name: Astrousia
blurb: This map is still a work in progress.

pointsOfInterest.name: Ankhet
pointsOfInterest.description: Ankhet combines a busy coastal economy with an enduring commitment to remembrance. Painters, stoneworkers, linen sellers, cooks, and boat crews share streets where funeral processions pass ordinary shops. The House of Names preserves household and burial records, while the Open Table feeds visiting families and offers temporary lodging. The Keeper of the Living Names, the city's sacred ruler, governs alongside institutions whose authority reaches into individual wards and households. In the Painted Ward, modest household markers stand beside commissions from wealthy patrons. Disputes over burial land, missing names, and the claims of living witnesses make remembrance a matter of everyday politics as well as devotion.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A working harbor renowned for painted memorials, public records, and the households that keep the names of the dead alive.

pointsOfInterest.name: CMC
pointsOfInterest.description:
Proposed identity only; the meaning of CMC remains unresolved.

The House combines practical observation, teaching, and hospitality. Roof catchments supply cisterns, and sheltered courts contain instruments and dated markers. Observers, maintenance workers, students, and their households sustain an institution dependent on regular supplies from lower settlements.
A College of Keepers administers the site. The Rain Court records measurements, while the Long Register preserves observations and accounts of exceptional storms. The Travelers’ Hall shelters people caught on the mountain approaches.
The House provides teaching, weather records, and route warnings in exchange for support. Its usefulness does not establish supernatural foresight, though residents may interpret their work through different religious traditions. Authorities seeking exclusive access to its observations face resistance from those who consider the records a shared resource.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Proposed identity: The House of Returning Rain. The House of Returning Rain maintains weather observations, mountain shelters, and warnings for travelers. Residents copy old records beside new measurements, preserving knowledge useful far beyond their walls. Access to those records has become a matter of political interest.

pointsOfInterest.name: Mount Oresh
pointsOfInterest.description:
Mount Oresh is both a landmark and a lived landscape. Communities on suitable lower slopes keep animals, maintain paths, and work small sources of stone. Their livelihoods connect them to lower settlements supplying grain, tools, and other necessities.
The Lower Shelters serve guides and travelers. The Broken Stair preserves an older engineered ascent whose original purpose remains uncertain. At the Weather Cairns, travelers leave reports for those following them. Those able to help customarily carry fuel, rope, or repair materials to the next shelter.
Authority varies between paths and communities, with local maintenance agreements often carrying more practical weight than distant claims. Quarrying concessions and attempts to control travel can threaten households dependent on established access.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Mount Oresh rises above the House of Returning Rain, crossed by difficult paths and marked with travelers’ cairns. Its slopes support scattered livelihoods and routes older than current border claims. Local communities dispute who may quarry it, guide across it, or close its paths.

pointsOfInterest.name: The Courts of Veyru
pointsOfInterest.description: The Courts of Veyru once served as an inland administrative and stopping place. Their surviving buildings belong to several periods: doorways were blocked, foundations reused, and inscriptions altered to suit later claims. The Court of Recut Names displays some of these changes openly, while the Lower Cisterns preserve successive repairs. Around the Pilgrims' Kitchen, seasonal visitors still maintain shelter and a hearth despite the collapse of neighboring structures. Local custodians, nearby households, and visiting researchers disagree over access and the removal of material. Veyru is a known place with living connections to its surroundings, and permission obtained in a distant city does not necessarily settle who may work there.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Well-known broken courts with recut inscriptions, repaired cisterns, and seasonal gathering places still tended by surrounding communities.

pointsOfInterest.name: Tameret
pointsOfInterest.description:
Tameret rises in broad terraces above a busy agricultural waterfront. Grain stores occupy the lower streets, while weaving courts and shaded homes climb behind them. Bakers feed early-shift porters flatbread filled with beans and onions, and freshly washed linen hangs above neighborhood courtyards.
A Council of Measures brings together farming districts, warehouse owners, and urban wards. Its most consequential decision is the annual grain reserve: how much food must remain locally available before unrestricted exports begin. Disputes over that reserve expose the divide between prosperous exporters and households dependent on affordable bread.
Official weights are tested publicly at the Measure Steps. The White Courts house linen workers and cloth merchants, while grain vessels load along First Loaf Quay. Tameret exports grain, pulses, linen, and sailcloth, relying on other communities for timber, salt, pottery, and metal tools. Djeskar’s shipyards are an important customer.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Tameret’s pale granaries and linen awnings overlook the gulf. Its agricultural hinterland supplies grain, cloth, and produce to neighboring ports. The city’s prosperity rests on an uneasy promise: exports must never leave its own people hungry.

pointsOfInterest.name: Djeskar
pointsOfInterest.description: Hammering carries across Djeskar's waterfront from dawn until dark. Its yards build fishing boats, merchant vessels, and warships, drawing timber, food, metal, and sailcloth from a wide network of suppliers. The Assembly of Yards shares public authority with the Bearer of the Keel Oath, the city's sacred ruler, while organized crews can halt the harbor through collective action. The Long Ways hold the principal slipways, the House of Soundings gathers navigators' reports, and the Unpaid Bell calls witnesses to wage disputes. Neighborhoods gather around their yards, sharing ovens and celebrating launches. Foreign commissions bring prosperity but also arguments about whose wars Djeskar's ships may eventually fight.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A shipbuilding city of crowded slipways, skilled crews, and powerful yards, where every launching is celebrated and unpaid wages remembered.

pointsOfInterest.name: Oseret
pointsOfInterest.description: Oseret gathers produce from the communities behind the western gulf shore. Livestock yards, shaded market courts, and independent warehouses allow small deliveries to become cargoes large enough for coastal trade. Its Witness-Crowned Sovereign holds sacred authority, while the Market Council and rural representatives negotiate the practical business of prices, storage, and access. At the Hundred Doors, merchants assemble goods from many households; at the Witness Court, spoken testimony may challenge a written contract. The Evening Market serves smaller buyers after the largest deals are concluded. Loans for seed, tools, and transport keep farms working, but poor harvests can turn a useful advance into a debt that outlives its borrower.
pointsOfInterest.summary: The western gulf's great market city, where growers, warehouse households, and lenders turn inland harvests into coastal trade.

pointsOfInterest.name: Kharaset
pointsOfInterest.description: Kharaset's streets open into caravan courts crowded with pack animals, wagons, repair shops, and travelers carrying news from the interior. Copper, salt, stone, and crafted goods pass through its weighing houses before reaching coastal buyers. The Guardian of the First Water embodies the city's sacred claim to protect passage and provision, alongside the Council of Gates and its competing commercial interests. At the Copper Court, assayers test metal and certify weights; at the Court of First Water, travelers receive a drink before lodging charges are discussed. Route communities retain their own wells and agreements. Kharaset's influence depends on those relationships, and ambitious toll collectors can threaten the trade they are meant to support.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A caravan and harbor city whose weighing courts, water customs, and repair workshops sustain the exchange between interior and coast.

pointsOfInterest.name: Isethra
pointsOfInterest.description: Isethra receives ocean travelers and prepares gulf vessels for distant voyages. Lantern Quay fills with unfamiliar cargo, returning crews, interpreters, and people waiting for news. The Patron of the Returning Light holds sacred authority, while the Harbor Compact binds the city to smaller ports that supply crews, provisions, and local knowledge. Shipping loans and cargo disputes come before the Exchange Courts. At the Returning Wall, families leave messages for absent sailors, sometimes renewing them for years. The city's prosperity depends on reliable services, freshwater, mainland food, and sound vessels. Smaller island communities value its rescue lights and commercial connections while resisting attempts to make every useful service compulsory.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Ilyra's principal harbor, sustained by pilots, interpreters, shipping houses, and the lights that guide crews home from the open sea.

pointsOfInterest.name: Caerulean
pointsOfInterest.description: Caerulean still carries the architectural imprint of Nwt's long rule: monumental approaches, blue ornament, government courts, and a harbor shaped to display sovereign power. Since the catastrophe of 58 BEC, markets have spread into ceremonial spaces and displaced households have rebuilt around surviving streets. Clerks continue to register births, property claims, and petitions beside damaged public buildings. The Harbor Secretariat coordinates essential services amid competing civic offices, neighborhood representatives, religious institutions, and a limited Beccin presence. The Blue Steps lead toward the administrative quarter, while the Court of Petitions hears demands for restitution. The city remains influential, but its continuing life has not settled who may legitimately inherit its former ruler's authority.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Nwt's former capital remains a major city of damaged ceremonial buildings, working offices, crowded markets, and disputed authority.

pointsOfInterest.name: The Namar Compact
pointsOfInterest.description:
The Namar Compact brings together communities with different interests and livelihoods. Some cultivate marine plants or tend shellfish grounds; others work in fishing, salvage, craft production, or diplomacy. Their agreements distinguish between passage above a place and activities that alter or remove what lies beneath it.
Delegates gather at the Listening Stones to hear disputes. The Nursery Grounds receive seasonal protection, while the Guest Moorings provide an agreed meeting place for surface vessels and merfolk envoys.
Surface residents often know the Compact through accounts of rescued sailors, returned anchors, or prohibited salvage. Its communities exchange marine products, services, and local knowledge for selected surface manufactures. Destructive anchoring, fishing disputes, and contested wrecks strain relations. Those suffering damage increasingly question whether negotiation alone protects their homes.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Beneath the gulf, the Namar Compact joins merfolk communities through agreements governing fisheries, cultivated seabeds, and wrecks. Its envoys negotiate with surface ports whose ships cross waters they rarely understand. This marker indicates an area of activity, not a capital or fixed border.

pointsOfInterest.name: Old Sounder’s Passage
pointsOfInterest.description:
Old Sounder is a sailors’ name, and accounts disagree about the creature’s habits and intentions. Its recurring visits may follow a feeding cycle or another need that surface observers have not understood. Pilots collect reports of surfacing, unusual wakes, and damaged vessels.
Sightings are recorded at the Witness Buoy. Captains gather at the Waiting Anchorage before deciding whether to proceed, paying close attention to witnesses whose livelihoods depend on accurate information.
Stories suggest an old understanding between Old Sounder, the Namar Compact, and former Nwt authorities. Whether such an agreement survives the Azure Sovereign’s fall remains uncertain. The creature’s appearances disrupt departures and convoy schedules, while accusations of exaggerated sightings divide pilots and shipping houses.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Sailors name these outer waters after Old Sounder, a dragon turtle reported here in certain seasons. Some crews delay departure when signs appear; others seek the creature deliberately. The marker records encounters rather than a permanent lair.

pointsOfInterest.name: Damietta
pointsOfInterest.description: Damietta surrounds a deep bay whose underwater dungeon helped establish the prestige of the Alhafar dynasty. Its rulers receive homage in a glass temple within greenish sandstone walls, maintaining a sacred kingship and a tradition of autonomy that survived Nwt's expansion. The Grand Bazaar trades everyday necessities alongside unusual recoveries from below, while Beergate's breweries supply the city's social life. Coffee and grapes grow in the farming district. At the Married Oysters, gambling and fighting pits draw travelers and residents alike. Beyond prosperous commercial streets, crowded households in Jungle's Edge negotiate the influence of the Panther's Paw and the pressure of surrounding vegetation. Maritime wealth supports the city without reaching every neighborhood equally.
pointsOfInterest.summary: An independent western port ruled by the Alhafar dynasty, famed for its glass temple, lively markets, breweries, and underwater dungeon.

pointsOfInterest.name: Khevaren
pointsOfInterest.description: Khevaren serves the settlements south of Ankhet, assembling small deliveries and providing storage, repairs, and lodging for carriers. Its familiar name, the Painted Measure, survives on colored market boards and the marked weights used to settle ordinary purchases. Potters, painters, and account keepers work beside households that combine trade with cultivation. The town has changed political masters without losing its usefulness as a place where goods can be counted, checked, and exchanged. Travelers find practical workshops and shared courtyards rather than monumental avenues. Local disputes usually concern access, tolls, damaged cargo, and whether an agreement witnessed in one generation still binds the next.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A modest town south of Ankhet, known as the Painted Measure for its market weights, decorated wares, and careful household accounts.

pointsOfInterest.name: Vaskeru
pointsOfInterest.description: Vaskeru stands northwest of Djeskar and serves the wider shipbuilding trade. Its Beam and Sail markets gather timber, cordage, cloth, and repair materials before they move onward to larger yards. Storage courts and eating houses support carriers and craft workers, while local households cultivate the ground needed to feed a town dependent on outside contracts. Older boundary stones survive beside repeatedly repaired streets, reminders of past struggles over the movement of valuable supplies. Today's merchants prefer predictable deliveries to grand territorial claims. A delayed payment or blocked route can still divide employers, workers, and growers over who must bear the cost of keeping business moving.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Known as Beam and Sail, Vaskeru gathers timber, cordage, and skilled labor for the shipbuilding economy around Djeskar.

pointsOfInterest.name: Eshoran
pointsOfInterest.description: Eshoran's Broadshade Market draws growers, livestock keepers, carriers, and household traders from the country northwest of Oseret. Its prosperity rests on assembling the small, irregular deliveries that larger merchants find inconvenient to collect themselves. Shaded courts provide space for bargaining and animal care, while lodging houses fill during the busiest market periods. Repaired paving and older property boundaries show how often its valuable commercial position has been contested. Residents judge distant authorities by the safety of access roads and the fairness of levies. Eshoran remains a town of working households and neighboring farms, even when its market days attract crowds large enough to suggest a much greater city.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A thriving market town northwest of Oseret, where shaded courts gather produce, pack animals, pottery, and news from surrounding communities.

pointsOfInterest.name: Rakhavel
pointsOfInterest.description: Rakhavel is still called Copperweight, although its active market now occupies only part of the space earlier generations maintained. Assayers, metal dealers, carriers, and repairers work among reused storehouses southwest of Kharaset. Its livelihood comes from checking and exchanging metal cargoes and repairing the equipment that moves them; the town's name does not imply a mine beneath its streets. Households supplement commercial work with other trades and local food production. Empty compounds and patched market walls make its diminished fortunes visible. Visitors can still obtain an experienced judgment on a suspect weight or damaged tool, provided they arrive when the right craft household is in residence.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A reduced but inhabited trading town southwest of Kharaset, where assayers, metal dealers, and repairers keep the Copperweight market working.

pointsOfInterest.name: Velithra
pointsOfInterest.description: Velithra supports Ilyra's maritime economy through work performed in courtyards, stores, and family workshops. Its Island Menders repair sails, cordage, clothing, and the smaller fittings that keep vessels useful between major refits. Food sellers and lodging households serve workers and customers moving through the island. Connections with Isethra bring business, but residents depend equally on agreements with smaller communities and independent crews. Public water points and shared storage are maintained through local contributions. The town's standing rests on dependable workmanship: a well-repaired sail is a lasting recommendation, while a hurried repair that fails at sea can become a dispute remembered across several harbors.
pointsOfInterest.summary: An inhabited town on Ilyra, known for sail repair, cordage, household workshops, and the practical skills of the Island Menders.

pointsOfInterest.name: Vaereth
pointsOfInterest.description: Vaereth's familiar name, Blue Plaster, recalls the decorated walls that once advertised its connections to Caerulean. It remains inhabited, though occupied houses and workshops now stand among compounds too large for the families maintaining them. Small-scale repair work, cultivation, and services for passing travelers support the remaining community. Residents reuse old masonry and keep a few common spaces functional rather than attempting to restore every abandoned room. The town's closeness to the former capital brings work as well as uncertainty over old obligations and property claims. For a traveler, Vaereth offers modest hospitality and practical knowledge of the surrounding country, with visible reminders of more prosperous times.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A struggling but inhabited town southwest of Caerulean, where surviving households repair older buildings beneath remnants of blue plaster.

pointsOfInterest.name: Daveret
pointsOfInterest.description: Daveret lies west of Damietta, where its Claybank Market connects household production with the demands of a much larger port. Potters, food sellers, carriers, and repairers exchange durable everyday goods rather than the spectacular finds celebrated in the city. Market courts double as places to arrange transport, locate relatives, and hear news of changing prices. Repeated repairs to older yards reflect a long history of storms, interrupted trade, and the maintenance of useful ground. Local households maintain their own agreements over water, work, and storage. Damietta's merchants are valuable customers, but bargaining with them is a regular necessity rather than an assurance of easy prosperity.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Damietta's western Claybank Market gathers pottery, provisions, and household goods for carriers moving between inland communities and the port.

pointsOfInterest.name: Amaleth
pointsOfInterest.description: Amaleth's Seven Courtyards give their name to a town whose activity gathers around a small number of maintained communal spaces. Households share ovens, arrange repairs, store modest cargoes, and accommodate travelers moving through the western country. Some older compounds stand partly empty, and market days are more important than the quiet streets between them might suggest. The town depends on nearby producers and reliable local arrangements rather than the wealth of a great harbor. Residents value news about the condition of routes and the availability of supplies. For outsiders, a host who knows the surrounding communities is often more useful than a merchant offering distant promises.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A small western town called Seven Courtyards, offering modest markets, shared ovens, repairs, and lodging along local exchange routes.

pointsOfInterest.name: Djaseret
pointsOfInterest.description: Djaseret remains a village despite the strength of its agricultural economy. Its Upper Reed Gardens support households whose work follows planting, water maintenance, harvest, and the preparation of produce for exchange. Communal stores and seed keeping help bridge poor seasons, while carriers connect local growers with larger markets. The village's importance comes from dependable food and experienced cultivators, not a monumental court or a large permanent garrison. Rights to plots and access to maintained water points are matters of close local attention. Visitors arriving at harvest encounter a busy settlement; at other times, the same households are dispersed among the gardens and their everyday maintenance work.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A prosperous agricultural village southeast of Oseret, where the Upper Reed Gardens support growers, seed keepers, and seasonal produce markets.

pointsOfInterest.name: Orenuva
pointsOfInterest.description: Orenuva preserves the name Southlake Exchange on a scale much smaller than its reputation might suggest. A limited group of households maintains storage space, a meeting court, and basic services for surrounding communities and occasional travelers. Trade arrives unevenly, so cultivation, repair work, and reciprocal help matter as much as coin or commercial cargo. Older foundations extend beyond the places now kept in regular use. Residents can arrange provisions and introduce visitors to people who know local routes, but large expeditions must bring their own support. Its continuing presence gives the southern country a familiar meeting point without making it a new regional capital.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A small southern settlement known as Southlake Exchange, where local households maintain a modest meeting place for provisions, repairs, and trade.

pointsOfInterest.name: Aleruva Quay
pointsOfInterest.description: Aleruva Quay is a familiar landmark in the country north of Djeskar. Its surviving stonework and silted waterworks preserve the outline of a landing place whose commercial functions moved elsewhere long ago. Domestic foundations behind the quay show that workers and their families once lived beside the movement of goods. Later sediment and repeated damage made the old arrangement increasingly difficult to read, but local guides can still identify several lines of construction. Visitors come to examine the masonry, compare old accounts, or use the place as a route marker. The site is remembered openly; its interest lies in the ordinary harbor life preserved beneath centuries of change.
pointsOfInterest.summary: An old quay north of Djeskar, recognizable by stranded masonry, silted waterworks, and the foundations of a vanished working neighborhood.

pointsOfInterest.name: Esholvar Yard
pointsOfInterest.description: Esholvar Yard, also remembered as Blueweight Yard, survives as a spread of working courts, domestic foundations, boundary stones, and partly silted channels. Its services eventually shifted to other establishments, leaving the older site to be reused piecemeal rather than rebuilt as a functioning town. Differences in paving and repairs reveal a longer history than its few standing walls suggest. People from the surrounding country know its position and use its conspicuous stones as landmarks. Craft workers and curious travelers visit to inspect old workmanship, while nearby households dispute the removal of useful material. It offers an approachable record of labor and exchange without the grandeur of a royal monument.
pointsOfInterest.summary: The remains of an old working yard northwest of Djeskar, with reused paving, household foundations, and channels from successive periods of activity.

pointsOfInterest.name: Orvakar Causeway
pointsOfInterest.description: Orvakar Causeway once supported a maintained crossing and the households that serviced it. Surviving stretches of raised road, boundary stones, and adjoining foundations show successive building campaigns rather than a single uninterrupted work. After an early abandonment, later inhabitants returned and repaired parts of the site before its permanent services disappeared again. Local travelers still know the route of the old causeway, although missing sections make its historical alignment easier to recognize than to follow. Visitors can see changes in road level and masonry without entering a hidden complex. The ruins are a reminder that even modest crossings could attract labor, tolls, settlement, and political rivalry.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A broken southern causeway whose raised road surfaces and old boundary stones remain familiar landmarks to local travelers.

pointsOfInterest.name: Omaluve Steps
pointsOfInterest.description: Omaluve Steps preserve the remains of a former landing and the small working settlement behind it. Broad masonry, altered channels, and domestic foundations mark a place rebuilt after one abandonment and eventually left without a permanent community again. The familiar name Reedline Steps survives among people who travel through the surrounding country. Seasonal growth and changing water conditions reveal different portions of the older works at different times. Visitors know where to find the site, but cannot assume that an ancient landing still provides a useful modern access point. Its surviving structures draw interest for the practical lives they reveal: storage, loading, shelter, and the repeated maintenance needed to keep exchange possible.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Ancient landing steps in the southern interior, bordered by ruined stores, old waterworks, and the traces of repeated rebuilding.

pointsOfInterest.name: Djenareth Quarry
pointsOfInterest.description: Djenareth Quarry contains worked faces, wedge holes, unfinished blocks, and the remains of routes used to move heavy stone. Earlier workings were abandoned and later reopened before the last resident establishment closed in 8 BEC. Stone remained in the landscape, but reaching and transporting worthwhile material beyond the serviced faces demanded more labor and provisioning than the operation could sustain. The site remains known to masons and carriers, and its recent closure preserves memories alongside older physical traces. Visitors can study the stages of cutting and movement in the exposed works. Occasional salvage does not amount to the return of a permanently staffed quarry settlement.
pointsOfInterest.summary: A well-known abandoned stone quarry with cut faces, unfinished blocks, lifting sockets, and haulways remembered by surviving craft traditions.

pointsOfInterest.name: Averet Kilns
pointsOfInterest.description: Averet Kilns preserve clay pits, firing floors, discarded batches, and broken channels from a long-lived pottery district. The works were abandoned, reopened centuries later, and finally lost their resident establishment in 122 BBEC. The practical problem was access to workable material within the district's supported reach, rather than the disappearance of every clay deposit in the region. Potters recognize useful lessons in the failed vessels and changing kiln layouts, while nearby communities remember the place as part of their working landscape. Seasonal visits and small-scale collection continue around an otherwise uninhabited site. Its ruins preserve everyday production rather than a lost palace or an undiscovered royal tomb.
pointsOfInterest.summary: Abandoned clay pits and kiln floors south of Ankhet, where broken firing batches record generations of ordinary pottery production.
